metadata.title: Conceptual inconsistencies in finite-dimensional quantum and classical mechanics

nodes.name: Self-consistent formulation of quantum mechanics in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space
nodes.statement: Hence, a self-consistent formulation of quantum mechanics in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space is an ongoing problem \cite{Weyl1950, Schwinger1960, Schwinger2003, Pearle1973, Santhanam1976, Jagannathan1981, Gudder1981, Jagannathan1982, Jagannathan1983, Gudder1985, Gudder1986, Busch1993, Galetti1999, Hakioglu2000, DelaTorre2003a, DelaTorre2003b, Vourdas2004, Gazeau2006, Revzen2008, Bang2009, Sasaki2011}, especially considering quantum information science, quantum optics, and physics of the Planck length, where finite-dimensionality finds new horizons.
nodes.statement_short: Building a self-consistent finite-dimensional formulation of quantum mechanics remains an open program.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.origin_citation: extensive prior literature, Weyl 1950 through Sasaki 2011

nodes.name: Weyl's equivalence between constant transition probability and the canonical commutation relation
nodes.statement: Utilizing group-theoretic arguments, Weyl demonstrated \cite{Weyl1950} \begin{align} \left| \langle x \ket{p} \right|^2 = \mbox{const} \Longleftrightarrow \commut{ \hat{x}, \hat{p} } = i \hbar, \end{align} (for alternative derivations see Refs. \cite{Schwinger2003, Bondar2011a}).
nodes.statement_short: Uniform coordinate-momentum transition probability is equivalent to the canonical commutation relation $[\hat{x},\hat{p}]=i\hbar$.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background

nodes.name: Nonexistence of bounded operators obeying the canonical commutation relation
nodes.statement: The left-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is well defined in a finite-dimensional space, whereas the right-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is not because no bounded operators obey the canonical commutation relation \cite{Weyl1950, Reed1980}.
nodes.statement_short: The commutator side of Weyl's equivalence fails in finite dimensions since no bounded operators satisfy the CCR.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
assumptions: no bounded operators obey the canonical commutation relation
conclusions: The left-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is well defined in a finite-dimensional space, whereas the right-hand side of Eq. (\ref{PhysOrigin_CCR}) is not

nodes.name: Coordinate and momentum operators via mutually unbiased bases
nodes.statement: Thus, in the literature on finite-dimensional quantum mechanics, the coordinate and momentum operators are usually defined as those whose eigenvectors obey \begin{align} \langle x_n \ket{p_k} = \exp(i2\pi n k /N) / \sqrt{N}, \end{align} where $n,k = -j, -j+1, \ldots, j-1, j$, $j =2N+1$, $\hat{x} \ket{x_n} = an\ket{x_n}$, $\hat{p} \ket{p_k} = 2\pi \hbar k/(aN) \ket{p_k}$, and $N$ is the Hilbert space's dimension (see Ref. \cite{DelaTorre2003a} for a detailed description of the notation). According to Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS}), the coordinate and momentum eigenvectors form mutually unbiased bases, which means that if a system is prepared in a state from one of the bases, then all outcomes of the measurement with respect to the other basis are equally probable.
nodes.statement_short: Finite-dimensional $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ are fixed by requiring their eigenbases to be mutually unbiased, with Fourier overlaps $\exp(i2\pi nk/N)/\sqrt{N}$.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
nodes.origin_citation: De la Torre & Goyeneche 2003; finite-dimensional quantum mechanics literature
nodes.genus: operators whose eigenvectors form mutually unbiased bases

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional Schr\"{o}dinger equation
nodes.statement: The finite-dimensional Schr\"{o}dinger equation is \begin{align} i\hbar \ket{d\Psi(t)/dt} = \hat{H} \ket{\Psi(t)}, \end{align} where there are at least two independent ways of introducing $\hat{H}$.
nodes.statement_short: The evolution equation $i\hbar\ket{d\Psi/dt} = \hat{H}\ket{\Psi}$ in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background

nodes.name: Tacit finite-dimensional Hamiltonian $\hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/(2m) + U(\hat{x})$
nodes.statement: First, the Hamiltonian \begin{align} \hat{H} = \hat{p}^2/(2m) + U(\hat{x}) \end{align} can be adapted with the specification that $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ are defined by Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS}). This is nearly a tacit definition of the Hamiltonian in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics.
nodes.statement_short: Take the infinite-dimensional form $\hat{p}^2/(2m)+U(\hat{x})$ with the mutually-unbiased-basis $\hat{x}$, $\hat{p}$.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
nodes.origin_citation: tacit definition in the finite-dimensional quantum mechanics literature

nodes.name: Finite-difference definition of the finite-dimensional Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: An alternative definition of $\hat{H}$, widely employed in numerical calculations (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Kimball1934}), is obtained once the term $\hat{p}^2/(2m)$, proportional to the second derivative in the infinite-dimensional coordinate representation, is approximated by finite differences. These two forms of the $N$-dimensional Hamiltonians are significantly different even though they converge to the same limit as $N \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Alternatively define $\hat{H}$ by replacing the kinetic term with a finite-difference approximation of the second derivative.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
differentia: the term $\hat{p}^2/(2m)$, proportional to the second derivative in the infinite-dimensional coordinate representation, is approximated by finite differences

nodes.name: Ehrenfest theorems
nodes.statement: In Ref. \cite{Bondar2011c}, along with a number of other applications, we utilized this method to infer the classical Liouville and Schr\"{o}dinger equations from the Ehrenfest theorems, \begin{align} m\frac{d}{dt} \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{x} \ket{\Psi(t)} & = \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{p} \ket{\Psi(t)}, \\ \frac{d}{dt} \bra{\Psi(t)} \hat{p} \ket{\Psi(t)} & = \bra{\Psi(t)} -U'(\hat{x}) \ket{\Psi(t)}, \end{align} by assuming that the coordinate $\hat{x}$ and momentum $\hat{p}$ commuted in the former case and obeyed the canonical commutation relation in the latter.
nodes.statement_short: The two Ehrenfest relations: $m\,d\langle\hat{x}\rangle/dt = \langle\hat{p}\rangle$ and $d\langle\hat{p}\rangle/dt = \langle -U'(\hat{x})\rangle$.
nodes.section: 2 Mathematical Background
nodes.origin_citation: Ehrenfest theorems; Bondar, Cabrera, Lompay, Ivanov & Rabitz 2011 (ODM)
assumptions: the coordinate $\hat{x}$ and momentum $\hat{p}$ commuted in the former case and obeyed the canonical commutation relation in the latter

nodes.name: Stone's theorem
nodes.statement: Stone's theorem (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Reed1980, Araujo2008}) guarantees the uniqueness of the Hermitian operator $\hat{H}$ in Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form}).
nodes.statement_short: The Hermitian generator $\hat{H}$ of a unitary evolution is unique.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
conclusions: the uniqueness of the Hermitian operator $\hat{H}$ in Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form})

nodes.name: Operator equations for the Hamiltonian implied by the Ehrenfest theorems
nodes.statement: Applying the chain rule to the left-hand side of Eqs. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}) and (\ref{EhrenfestTh2}) and then utilizing Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form}), one obtains \begin{align} im \commut{\hat{H}, \hat{x}} &= \hbar \hat{p}, \\ i\commut{\hat{H}, \hat{p}} &= -\hbar U'(\hat{x}). \end{align} We shall demonstrate below that Eqs. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) cannot be satisfied by non-trivial finite-dimensional operators.
nodes.statement_short: ODM converts the Ehrenfest theorems into the commutator equations $im[\hat{H},\hat{x}]=\hbar\hat{p}$ and $i[\hat{H},\hat{p}]=-\hbar U'(\hat{x})$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (nonexistence of the free particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics)
nodes.statement: Assume $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{H}$ are non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators. If $\commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{p} } = 0$ then there is no finite-dimensional linear operator $\hat{x}$ such that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: If a finite-dimensional Hermitian $\hat{H}$ commutes with a non-zero $\hat{p}$, no $\hat{x}$ can satisfy the first Ehrenfest relation.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
assumptions: $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{H}$ are non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators
conclusions: there is no finite-dimensional linear operator $\hat{x}$ such that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Let $\ket{E_n}$ denote a joint eigenvector of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$ such that $\hat{H} \ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$ and $\hat{p} \ket{E_n} = p_n \ket{E_n}$. Assuming that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$, one obtains \begin{align} i \bra{E_n} \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } \ket{E_m} = i (E_n - E_m) \bra{E_n} \hat{x} \ket{E_m} = p_m \langle E_n \ket{E_m}, \end{align} $\forall n,m$. The special case of this identity, when $n=m$, reads $p_m = 0$, $\forall m$. This contradicts the assumption that $\hat{p}$ is a non-zero matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich the assumed commutator identity between joint eigenvectors of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$; the diagonal case forces $p_m=0$, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Introduce joint eigenvectors of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$
nodes.statement: Let $\ket{E_n}$ denote a joint eigenvector of $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$ such that $\hat{H} \ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$ and $\hat{p} \ket{E_n} = p_n \ket{E_n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the common eigenbasis available because $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{p}$ commute.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Sandwich the commutator identity between eigenvectors
nodes.statement: Assuming that $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$, one obtains \begin{align} i \bra{E_n} \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{x} } \ket{E_m} = i (E_n - E_m) \bra{E_n} \hat{x} \ket{E_m} = p_m \langle E_n \ket{E_m}, \end{align} $\forall n,m$.
nodes.statement_short: Take matrix elements of the assumed identity, yielding $i(E_n-E_m)\bra{E_n}\hat{x}\ket{E_m} = p_m \langle E_n\ket{E_m}$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Diagonal case yields the contradiction
nodes.statement: The special case of this identity, when $n=m$, reads $p_m = 0$, $\forall m$. This contradicts the assumption that $\hat{p}$ is a non-zero matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Set $n=m$ to get $p_m=0$ for all $m$, contradicting $\hat{p} \neq 0$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Physical reading of Theorem 1: confinement and the definition of the confining force
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} physically implies the nonexistence of the ``free'' particle in finite-dimensional quantum mechanics. This statement is also a consequence of probability conservation, closely linked to Stone's theorem. If the wave function's normalization is constant and $\hat{x}$ is finite-dimensional, then the particle's motion is confined to the spatial interval bound by the smallest and largest eigenvalues of $\hat{x}$. This confinement must be realized by some force. Since standalone Eq. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) is solvable with respect to $\hat{H}$ [see Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) below], then $i \commut{ \hat{H}, \hat{p} }/\hbar$ from Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) can be taken as the definition of this confining force. Note that the Ehrenfest theorems do not hold for a particle in a box even in the infinite-dimensional case \cite{Alonso2000}.
nodes.statement_short: Finite-dimensionality confines the particle between the extreme eigenvalues of $\hat{x}$, and $i[\hat{H},\hat{p}]/\hbar$ can serve as the confining force.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (a derivative cannot be represented as a commutator in finite dimensions)
nodes.statement: There are no finite-dimensional operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ such that \begin{align} \commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A}) \end{align} for any ``good'' function $f(z)$.
nodes.statement_short: No finite-dimensional pair $(\hat{A},\hat{B})$ realizes differentiation as the commutator $[f(\hat{A}),\hat{B}] = f'(\hat{A})$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
conclusions: There are no finite-dimensional operators $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{B}$ such that \begin{align} \commut{ f(\hat{A}), \hat{B} } = f'(\hat{A}) \end{align}

nodes.name: Function of an operator via Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Let a function of an operator be defined as (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Nazaikinskii1992}) \begin{align} f(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \quad f'(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int ik g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \notag \end{align} where $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$.
nodes.statement_short: $f(\hat{A})$ is defined by integrating $e^{ik\hat{A}}$ against the Fourier transform $g(k)$ of $f$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
differentia: $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let a function of an operator be defined as (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Nazaikinskii1992}) \begin{align} f(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \quad f'(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int ik g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \notag \end{align} where $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$. The correctness of Eq. (\ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Eq1}) implies \begin{align} \commut{ e^{ik\hat{A}}, \hat{B} } = ik e^{ik\hat{A}}. \end{align} Differentiating the last identity with respect to $k$ and setting $k=0$, we reach the contradiction $\commut{ \hat{A}, \hat{B} } = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the Fourier representation of $f(\hat{A})$, differentiate the resulting exponential identity at $k=0$, and land on the forbidden relation $[\hat{A},\hat{B}]=1$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Adopt the Fourier definition of a function of an operator
nodes.statement: Let a function of an operator be defined as (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Nazaikinskii1992}) \begin{align} f(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \quad f'(\hat{A}) \coloneqq \int ik g(k) e^{ik\hat{A}} dk, \notag \end{align} where $g(k)$ is the Fourier transform of a function $f(z)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the operator-function calculus used in the argument.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Reduce the hypothesis to an exponential commutator identity
nodes.statement: The correctness of Eq. (\ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Eq1}) implies \begin{align} \commut{ e^{ik\hat{A}}, \hat{B} } = ik e^{ik\hat{A}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The assumed relation must hold for each exponential mode: $[e^{ik\hat{A}},\hat{B}] = ik e^{ik\hat{A}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Differentiate at $k=0$ to reach the contradiction
nodes.statement: Differentiating the last identity with respect to $k$ and setting $k=0$, we reach the contradiction $\commut{ \hat{A}, \hat{B} } = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiating at $k=0$ forces the canonical relation $[\hat{A},\hat{B}]=1$, impossible for finite matrices.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Two nonequivalent definitions of a potential force $\hat{F}$
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NoDiffAsCommutator_Theorem} establishes not only the nonsolvability of Eq. (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) but also two nonequivalent definitions ($\hat{F} = - U'(\hat{x})$ and $\hat{F} = i\commut{U(\hat{x}), \hat{p}}/\hbar$) of a potential force $\hat{F}$ in a finite-dimensional framework. The latter definition should be preferred due to the comment after Theorem \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem}.
nodes.statement_short: In finite dimensions the potential force admits two inequivalent definitions, and the commutator one is preferable.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Liouvillian $\hat{L}$ as the classical dynamics' generator
nodes.statement: As thoroughly elaborated in Ref. \cite{Bondar2011c}, the Liouvillian $\hat{L}$, the classical dynamics' generator, is a solution of the equations: $im\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$ and $i\commut{\hat{L}, \hat{p}} = -U'(\hat{x})$ with commuting $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: The classical generator $\hat{L}$ solves the same pair of commutator equations, but with commuting $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
differentia: a solution of the equations: $im\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$ and $i\commut{\hat{L}, \hat{p}} = -U'(\hat{x})$

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (nonexistence of a finite-dimensional Liouvillian)
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ be non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators with $\commut{\hat{x}, \hat{p}} = 0$. There is no finite-dimensional operator $\hat{L}$ such that $i\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: Finite-dimensional classical mechanics has no Liouvillian satisfying the first Ehrenfest relation.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics
assumptions: Let $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{p}$ be non-zero finite-dimensional Hermitian operators with $\commut{\hat{x}, \hat{p}} = 0$
conclusions: There is no finite-dimensional operator $\hat{L}$ such that $i\commut{ \hat{L}, \hat{x} } = \hat{p}$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Up to the notation ($\hat{H} \leftrightarrow \hat{x}$ and $\hat{x} \leftrightarrow \hat{L}$), this theorem is the same as Theorem \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem}.
nodes.statement_short: Relabel the operators and quote Theorem 1.
nodes.section: 3 Revealing Inconsistencies in Finite-dimensional Quantum and Classical Mechanics

nodes.name: Universality of the numerical-accuracy conclusions
nodes.statement: We shall now show that the accuracy of numerical calculations appears not to depend on whether a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian obeys the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}). Even though we analyze a specific system with a few different choices for its Hamiltonian, the conclusions are universal because the root of the problem lies in the nonexistence of bounded operators obeying the canonical commutation relation.
nodes.statement_short: Numerical accuracy is insensitive to whether the Hamiltonian obeys the first Ehrenfest theorem, and this is universal.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
assumptions: the root of the problem lies in the nonexistence of bounded operators obeying the canonical commutation relation
conclusions: the accuracy of numerical calculations appears not to depend on whether a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian obeys the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})

nodes.name: Most general Hamiltonian obeying the first Ehrenfest theorem
nodes.statement: Assuming $\hat{x}$ is Hermitian and has a non-degenerate spectrum, the solution of Eq. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) is \begin{align} \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star} \ket{x_l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} U(x_k) + C & \mbox{if } k=l \\ \frac{i \hbar \bra{x_k} \hat{p} \ket{x_l} }{m(x_k - x_l)} &\mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \end{align} where $\hat{x} \ket{x_l} = x_l \ket{x_l}$ and $C$ is an arbitrary real constant. For any definition of the momentum operator $\hat{p}$, Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) provides the most general Hamiltonian obeying the first Ehrenfest theorem [Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})].
nodes.statement_short: For non-degenerate Hermitian $\hat{x}$, the general first-Ehrenfest-compatible Hamiltonian has diagonal $U(x_k)+C$ and off-diagonal $i\hbar\bra{x_k}\hat{p}\ket{x_l}/[m(x_k-x_l)]$.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
assumptions: $\hat{x}$ is Hermitian and has a non-degenerate spectrum
For any definition of the momentum operator $\hat{p}$
conclusions: the solution of Eq. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) is \begin{align} \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star} \ket{x_l} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} U(x_k) + C & \mbox{if } k=l \\ \frac{i \hbar \bra{x_k} \hat{p} \ket{x_l} }{m(x_k - x_l)} &\mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \end{align}
Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) provides the most general Hamiltonian obeying the first Ehrenfest theorem [Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})]

nodes.name: Finite-difference momentum operator $\hat{p}_{fd}$
nodes.statement: Choosing $\hat{x}$ with equally spaced eigenvalues (with the step $a$) and utilizing the approximation $d \Psi(x_k) /dx \approx [ \Psi(x_{k+1}) - \Psi(x_{k-1}) ] / (2a)$, we can define the momentum operator: $\bra{x_k} \hat{p}_{fd} \ket{x_l} = -i\hbar\left( \delta_{l,k+1} - \delta_{l,k-1} \right)/(2a)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\hat{p}_{fd}$ is the centered finite-difference momentum matrix on an equally spaced coordinate grid.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
differentia: $\hat{x}$ with equally spaced eigenvalues (with the step $a$)

nodes.name: Ehrenfest-compatible finite-difference Hamiltonian $\hat{H}^{\star}_{fd}$
nodes.statement: Then, the corresponding Hamiltonian from Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}), \begin{align} \bra{x_k} \hat{H}^{\star}_{fd} \ket{x_l} = \frac{-\hbar^2}{2ma^2} \left( \delta_{l,k+1} + \delta_{l,k-1} \right) + [U(x_k) + C]\delta_{l,k}, \end{align} satisfying the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}), takes the form of the simplest finite-difference approximation for the differential operator: $-\hbar^2/(2m) d^2/dx^2 + U(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Substituting $\hat{p}_{fd}$ into the general solution reproduces the standard three-point finite-difference Hamiltonian.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations

nodes.name: Hamiltonians $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ and $\hat{H}_{mub}$
nodes.statement: Let $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ denote the Hamiltonian (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) after substituting $\hat{p}$ from Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS}), and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ be the Hamiltonian (\ref{Infinite_Dim_Form_Hamiltonian}) with the same $\hat{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: Two mutually-unbiased-basis Hamiltonians: the Ehrenfest-compatible $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ and the naive $\hat{H}_{mub}$.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
differentia: the Hamiltonian (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian}) after substituting $\hat{p}$ from Eq. (\ref{Deff_PX_as_MUBS})

nodes.name: $\hat{H}_{mub}$ violates the first Ehrenfest theorem
nodes.statement: Contrary to $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, the matrix $\hat{H}_{mub}$ does not satisfy the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}).
nodes.statement_short: The naive mutually-unbiased-basis Hamiltonian fails the first Ehrenfest theorem.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
assumptions: $\hat{H}_{mub}$ be the Hamiltonian (\ref{Infinite_Dim_Form_Hamiltonian}) with the same $\hat{p}$
conclusions: the matrix $\hat{H}_{mub}$ does not satisfy the Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})

nodes.name: Singular harmonic oscillator potential
nodes.statement: \begin{align} U(x) = \frac{\omega^2}{8} x^2 + \frac{g}{4x^2}, \qquad 0 \leqslant x < \infty, \end{align} which is exactly solvable in the infinite-dimensional case \cite{Calogero1969}.
nodes.statement_short: The exactly solvable singular oscillator potential $\omega^2 x^2/8 + g/(4x^2)$ on the half-line.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations

nodes.name: Numerical comparison of $\hat{H}^{\star}_{fd}$, $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ for the singular harmonic oscillator
nodes.statement: Figures \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison} and \ref{Fig_EigenvectorComparison} depict the eigenvalues and the twentieth eigenvector of the Hamiltonians $\hat{H}^{\star}_{fd}$, $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ for the oscillator, \begin{align} U(x) = \frac{\omega^2}{8} x^2 + \frac{g}{4x^2}, \qquad 0 \leqslant x < \infty, \end{align} which is exactly solvable in the infinite-dimensional case \cite{Calogero1969}. The values of the coordinate step, $a$, for $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ are selected to minimize the largest eigenvalues of each Hamiltonian, which leads to the spectra of $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ and $\hat{H}_{mub}$ (for a finite $N$) best fitting the exact energy in the infinite-dimensional case [see Figs. \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison}(b) and \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison}(c)]. However, the same recipe applied to $\hat{H}_{fd}^{\star}$ does not provide a good fit, and the step size for $\hat{H}_{fd}^{\star}$ is manually adjusted to match the exact energies. This exercise demonstrates [Fig. \ref{Fig_EigenvectorComparison}(a)] that even though the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{fd}^{\star}$ reproduces the exact energy better than either $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$ or $\hat{H}_{mub}$, it yields poor quality excited states. Finally, note that the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{mub}^{\star}$, satisfying Ehrenfest theorem (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}), provides results of the same quality as $\hat{H}_{mub}$, violating Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}). These observations indicate that there is no correlation between the numerical calculations' accuracy and the Ehrenfest theorem's validity. Note, however, that any disagreement between the exact and numerical results in Figs. \ref{Fig_SpectraComparison} and \ref{Fig_EigenvectorComparison} will exponentially increase with the number of spatial dimensions.
nodes.statement_short: A 30-dimensional numerical study of the singular oscillator comparing spectra and the twentieth eigenvector for the three candidate Hamiltonians.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations

nodes.name: No correlation between numerical accuracy and the Ehrenfest theorem's validity
nodes.statement: These observations indicate that there is no correlation between the numerical calculations' accuracy and the Ehrenfest theorem's validity.
nodes.statement_short: Obeying the Ehrenfest theorem does not improve numerical accuracy.
nodes.section: 4 Inconsistencies and Numerical Calculations
conclusions: there is no correlation between the numerical calculations' accuracy and the Ehrenfest theorem's validity

nodes.name: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians as a candidate fix
nodes.statement: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians are widely employed to model resonant and unbound states (see, e.g., Refs. \cite{Moiseyev2011, Graefe2011} and references therein) as well as a handy trick to avoid numerical artifacts related to the finiteness of spatial grids (see, e.g., Ref. \cite{Manolopoulos2002}). The Hamiltonian's non-Hermitianity leads to non-conservation of the wave function's normalization. The normalization decreasing over time is interpreted as a quantum particle leaving the spatial interval bound by the coordinate's smallest and largest eigenvalues. Therefore, it might be anticipated that this will at least restore the free particle's notion. Despite great utility, non-Hermitian Hamiltonians do not resolve the conceptual difficulties, as we shall demonstrate now.
nodes.statement_short: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians relax normalization conservation and might be hoped to restore the free particle, but they do not fix the inconsistencies.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Non-Hermitian generalizations of the ODM operator equations
nodes.statement: First, re-applying ODM to Eqs. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1}) and (\ref{EhrenfestTh2}) with the condition $\hat{H} \neq \hat{H}^{\dagger}$, the following generalizations of Eqs. (\ref{First_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_CommutEq_for_Hamiltonian}) are obtained: \begin{align} im ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{x} - \hat{x} \hat{H} ) = \hbar \hat{p}, \quad i ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{p} - \hat{p} \hat{H} ) = -\hbar U'(\hat{x}). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: For $\hat{H} \neq \hat{H}^{\dagger}$ the commutators are replaced by $\hat{H}^{\dagger}\hat{A} - \hat{A}\hat{H}$ expressions.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (disjoint spectra force $\hat{p} = \hat{x} = 0$)
nodes.statement: Assume that $\hat{x}$, $\hat{p}$, and $\hat{H}$ are bounded. If $\sigma(\hat{H}^{\dagger}) \cap \sigma(\hat{H}) = \emptyset$ and \begin{align} & im ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{x} - \hat{x} \hat{H} ) = \hbar \hat{p}, \\ & \hat{H}^{\dagger} \hat{p} = \hat{p} \hat{H}, \end{align} then $\hat{p} = \hat{x} = 0$. Here, $\sigma(\hat{A})$ denotes the spectrum of an operator $\hat{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: For bounded operators with $\sigma(\hat{H}^{\dagger})$ and $\sigma(\hat{H})$ disjoint, the non-Hermitian Ehrenfest equations only admit the trivial solution.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: First, we employ the Rosenblum theorem \cite{Rosenblum1956} (see Theorem 9.3 in Ref. \cite{Bhatia1997}) to Eq. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and then employ Eq. (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) to show \begin{align} im\hat{x} =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} - \xi )^{-1} \hat{p} ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-1} \notag\\ =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \hat{p} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-2} = 0, \end{align} where $\Gamma$ denotes a union of closed contours in the complex plane with total winding numbers $1$ around $\sigma(\hat{H}^{\dagger})$ and $0$ around $\sigma(\hat{H})$.
nodes.statement_short: Represent $\hat{x}$ by the Rosenblum contour-integral formula, commute $\hat{p}$ through, and observe the resulting resolvent-squared contour integral vanishes.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Apply the Rosenblum theorem
nodes.statement: First, we employ the Rosenblum theorem \cite{Rosenblum1956} (see Theorem 9.3 in Ref. \cite{Bhatia1997}) to Eq. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian})
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Rosenblum's contour-integral solution of the Sylvester-type operator equation.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Collapse the contour integral to zero
nodes.statement: and then employ Eq. (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) to show \begin{align} im\hat{x} =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H}^{\dagger} - \xi )^{-1} \hat{p} ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-1} \notag\\ =& \frac{\hbar}{2\pi i} \hat{p} \oint_{\Gamma} d\xi ( \hat{H} - \xi )^{-2} = 0, \end{align} where $\Gamma$ denotes a union of closed contours in the complex plane with total winding numbers $1$ around $\sigma(\hat{H}^{\dagger})$ and $0$ around $\sigma(\hat{H})$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\hat{H}^{\dagger}\hat{p} = \hat{p}\hat{H}$ to pull $\hat{p}$ out, leaving a vanishing $(\hat{H}-\xi)^{-2}$ contour integral.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Theorem 4 (no free particle in non-Hermitian finite-dimensional mechanics)
nodes.statement: Assume i) $\hat{H}$, $\hat{x}$, and $\hat{p}$ are finite-dimensional operators satisfying Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}); ii) $\lim_{t \to +\infty} \left| \langle \Psi(t) \ket{\Psi(t)} \right| < \infty$, where $\ket{\Psi(t)}$ is a solution of Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form}); iii) the eigenvectors $\{ \ket{E_n} \}_{n=1}^N$ ($\hat{H}\ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$, $n \in I \coloneqq \{1,2,\ldots,N\}$) span the entire Hilbert space. Then, $\hat{p} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Even with a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, a bounded-norm diagonalizable finite-dimensional model satisfying the Ehrenfest equations forces $\hat{p}=0$.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies
assumptions: $\hat{H}$, $\hat{x}$, and $\hat{p}$ are finite-dimensional operators satisfying Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian})
$\lim_{t \to +\infty} \left| \langle \Psi(t) \ket{\Psi(t)} \right| < \infty$, where $\ket{\Psi(t)}$ is a solution of Eq. (\ref{Sch_Eq_General_Form})
the eigenvectors $\{ \ket{E_n} \}_{n=1}^N$ ($\hat{H}\ket{E_n} = E_n \ket{E_n}$, $n \in I \coloneqq \{1,2,\ldots,N\}$) span the entire Hilbert space

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Suppose $\hat{p} \neq 0$. According to Lyapunov stability theory \cite{Lyapunov1992}, the second assumption implies that $\Im(E_n) \leqslant 0$, $\forall n\in I$. Lemma \ref{NonHermitian_Lemma1} guarantees that $\hat{H}$ has at least a single real eigenvalue. Introduce $R \coloneqq \{ n \in I \, | \, \Im(E_n) = 0 \} \neq \emptyset$ -- the set of the real eigenvalues' indices. ``Sandwiching'' Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) leads to \begin{align} & im ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{x} \ket{E_l} = \hbar \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}, \\ & ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0, \qquad \forall k,l \in I. \end{align} According to Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq2}), $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}$ may be non-zero only for $(k,l) \in Q \coloneqq \{ (k,l) \in R \times R \, | \, E_k = E_l \}$. However, Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq1}) enforces $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0$, $\forall (k,l) \in Q$. Therefore, we reach the contradiction $\hat{p} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\hat{p} \neq 0$, restrict to the real part of the spectrum via Lyapunov stability and Lemma 1, then sandwich the operator equations to kill every matrix element of $\hat{p}$.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Assume $\hat{p} \neq 0$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\hat{p} \neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Open the argument by contradiction.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Bound the imaginary parts of the eigenvalues
nodes.statement: According to Lyapunov stability theory \cite{Lyapunov1992}, the second assumption implies that $\Im(E_n) \leqslant 0$, $\forall n\in I$.
nodes.statement_short: Norm boundedness plus Lyapunov stability theory gives $\Im(E_n) \leqslant 0$ for all $n$.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Extract the non-empty set of real eigenvalues via Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{NonHermitian_Lemma1} guarantees that $\hat{H}$ has at least a single real eigenvalue. Introduce $R \coloneqq \{ n \in I \, | \, \Im(E_n) = 0 \} \neq \emptyset$ -- the set of the real eigenvalues' indices.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 1 forces at least one real eigenvalue, so the index set $R$ of real eigenvalues is non-empty.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Sandwich the operator equations between eigenvectors
nodes.statement: ``Sandwiching'' Eqs. (\ref{First_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) and (\ref{Second_OperEq_for_NonHer_FreeHamiltonian}) leads to \begin{align} & im ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{x} \ket{E_l} = \hbar \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}, \\ & ( E_k^* - E_l ) \bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0, \qquad \forall k,l \in I. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Take matrix elements of both non-Hermitian operator equations in the eigenbasis of $\hat{H}$.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Every matrix element of $\hat{p}$ vanishes
nodes.statement: According to Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq2}), $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l}$ may be non-zero only for $(k,l) \in Q \coloneqq \{ (k,l) \in R \times R \, | \, E_k = E_l \}$. However, Eq. (\ref{NonHermTh1_Eq1}) enforces $\bra{E_k} \hat{p} \ket{E_l} = 0$, $\forall (k,l) \in Q$. Therefore, we reach the contradiction $\hat{p} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The surviving index pairs are exactly those the first equation annihilates, so $\hat{p} = 0$.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Theorem 4 generalizes Theorems 1 and 3
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{NonHermitian_Theorem1}, being a generalization of Theorems \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} and \ref{NoFiniteDimClassicalMecahnics}, disproves the existence of the free quantum and classical particle within a non-Hermitian setting.
nodes.statement_short: The non-Hermitian theorem subsumes the Hermitian and classical no-go results.
nodes.section: 5 Non-Hermitian Hamiltonian as an Unsuccessful Attempt to Fix Inconsistencies

nodes.name: Summary of the established inconsistencies
nodes.statement: Utilizing ODM \cite{Bondar2011c}, we demonstrated that {\it all} finite-dimensional representations of quantum and classical dynamics violate the second Ehrenfest theorem [Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh2})], while the first Ehrenfest theorem [Eq. (\ref{EhrenfestTh1})] may be satisfied under special circumstances [Eq. (\ref{Ehrenfest_Compartible_GeneralHamiltonian})]. Nonexistence of the free particle case and the ambiguity in defining potential forces were also established. The fundamental reason behind these inconsistencies is the absence of bounded operators obeying the canonical commutation relation. These conclusions fundamentally bound the accuracy achievable by the current paradigm of numerical simulations.
nodes.statement_short: All finite-dimensional dynamics violate the second Ehrenfest theorem; the first can hold only in special cases, and the root cause is the absence of bounded CCR operators.
nodes.section: 6 Outlook

nodes.name: Circumventing the no-go theorems via nonstandard analysis
nodes.statement: In particular, a key element in proving theorems \ref{NoFreeFiniteDimQM_Theorem} and \ref{NoFiniteDimClassicalMecahnics} is the non-existence of a finite real number $r$ such that $0\cdot r \neq 0$. However, this equation has a solution if infinitesimal and infinitely-large numbers are included into the set of real numbers. Thus, some of the no-go theorems may be avoided by utilizing nonstandard analysis \cite{robert2003nonstandard, Almeida2004}, where such extensions are rigorously implemented. An adaptation of the latter approach to physical simulations would be a computational paradigm shift.
nodes.statement_short: Whether nonstandard analysis, with infinitesimals admitting $0\cdot r \neq 0$, can be adapted to physical simulations and evade the no-go theorems.
